questions.question: Define inflation so that all three tests in the definition are visible, and describe the four stages by which Statistics South Africa builds the CPI, explaining the purpose of the basket, the weights and the base year.
questions.expected_answer: Inflation is a sustained and significant increase in the general price level over time. Sustained excludes once-off jumps such as a single fuel-levy increase; general excludes relative price changes where one product rises while others fall; over time means the rise is measured against an earlier period, usually the same month a year before. The CPI is built in four stages. First, household expenditure surveys establish the basket — several hundred items households genuinely buy, from maize meal to prepaid electricity and data bundles. Second, each item receives a weight equal to its share of total household spending: housing and utilities roughly a quarter, food and non-alcoholic drinks a little under a fifth, transport around a seventh. Third, collectors record tens of thousands of prices every month across the country. Fourth, the weighted average is expressed as an index with the base year set at 100, so an index of 108 means what cost R100 in the base year costs R108 now. Headline CPI covers all items; core inflation strips out volatile food, fuel and energy; the PPI, priced at the factory gate, acts as an early warning of pressure heading for the CPI.

questions.question: The CPI climbs from 108,0 to 114,5 over a year. Calculate the inflation rate, name the two classic calculation traps, and comment on a nurse whose salary rose 5 percent over the same year.
questions.expected_answer: Inflation rate = (new index − old index) ÷ old index × 100 = (114,5 − 108,0) ÷ 108,0 × 100 = 6,5 ÷ 108,0 × 100 = 6,02%, approximately 6,0%. Trap one is dividing by the new index instead of the old: a rate measures growth from where the year began, just as a bus ticket rising from R20 to R25 is a 25 percent increase on the R20 you used to pay. Trap two is reporting index points as the rate: the index moved 6,5 points, but the inflation rate is 6,0 percent, and points are not percentages. The nurse received 5 percent nominally while prices rose about 6 percent, so her real salary fell by roughly 1 percent — she earns more rands but they fill a smaller trolley, which is why wage negotiations are benchmarked against the CPI.

questions.question: Distinguish demand-pull from cost-push inflation, using the curve stories, and evaluate inflation targeting through the repo rate as South Africa's main response, stating clearly which type it fights well and which it fights badly.
questions.expected_answer: Demand-pull inflation starts on the spending side: total demand grows faster than the economy can produce, driven by cheap credit, consumer and investment booms, government deficits or export surges. Aggregate demand shifts right along aggregate supply — prices and output both rise, with busy shops and sold-out stock as symptoms. Cost-push inflation starts on the production side: input costs rise and are passed on — wage settlements outrunning productivity, a weaker rand raising import costs, fuel and electricity increases, drought-driven food prices. Aggregate supply shifts left — prices rise while output falls, producing stagflation. Since 2000 the Reserve Bank has been mandated to keep CPI inflation in a 3-to-6-percent band using the repo rate: raising it lifts all lending rates, cools borrowing and spending, and anchors expectations, while the Bank's independence prevents money being printed for the state. The framework fights demand-pull inflation well because it attacks excess demand directly. It fights cost-push inflation badly because higher interest rates cannot lower a single production cost — they only suppress demand around the shock, sacrificing output and jobs, the trade-off the Phillips curve captures. A strong answer adds supporting measures — fiscal restraint, moderating administered prices, and competition and productivity policies that grow supply — and notes that direct wage and price controls tend to fail by breeding shortages and black markets.
